To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the developmental trajectories of alcohol use and alcohol problems are highly variable, with some individuals showing a stable trajectory of low alcohol use and low alcohol problems, others a stable trajectory of high use and high problems, and others a trajectory of high initial use and problems that decline over time.

(1) early childhood temperament and affective control are predictive of later alcohol and drug use and problems, (2) parental disruptive behavior disorders and their associated child rearing practices predict adolescent onset and course of alcohol use and problems, and (3) early adult trajectories of alcohol use and abuse predict later alcohol abuse and dependence.

(1) the ability to predict alcohol problems and alcohol and other substance use disorders is greatest for children and adolescents, (2) the predictive ability of early indicators is greatest for alcohol and other substance problems in the short term and for alcohol problems in the long term, (3) the predictive utility of early indicators of alcohol problems is greater than the predictive ability of alcohol problems themselves, and (4) early predictors of alcohol problems are not necessarily early indicators of alcoholism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the development and maintenance of alcohol problems and the causes of alcohol use disorder.
understanding the causes and course (including the prevention and treatment) of alcohol problems, including alcohol use disorder.
the development of alcohol problems and the causes and course thereof.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the case of the developmental trajectories of risky drinking and alcohol problems, it is possible to get advance notice from as early as toddlerhood to middle adulthood, and this is a very good thing for the prevention of alcohol problems and related problems in adulthood.

we can get some advance notice of risky drinking and substance use disorder outcomes, but that this notice is not perfect, and that the further ahead in development we try to look, the more limited our advance warning is likely to be.
the developmental course of alcohol problems can be predicted with increasing accuracy as the time interval between the prediction and the target outcome increases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more we know about the developmental context in which a person is functioning, the more we can predict the future.

we can get some advance notice about alcohol problems, and that such notice can be used to inform our understanding of the etiology and course of alcohol use disorder and to guide the development of more effective preventive interventions.

we have been able to predict alcohol problems with a fair amount of success, but we are not able to do so with the same degree of accuracy across the developmental span from childhood to early adulthood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the earlier in development one begins to assess and treat alcohol problems, the better.
, while there is a great deal we can learn about alcohol problems and alcohol-related disorders from the study of developmental processes, we still have a great deal to learn.

the developmental course of alcohol use disorders can be anticipated and, in some cases, predicted from very early childhood, with the degree of predictability increasing as the age of the target increases.
